texts.1.1: The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley
texts.2.1: The poetical publications of John and Charles Wesley originally appeared at various intervals during a space of fifty-two or -three years. The total number of them, as far as at present ascertained, is fifty-seven; of which, seven bore the names of the two brothers, seven of John Wesley only, eight of Charles Wesley only; while the remaining thirty-five were anonymous, though some were afterwards owned, and all are capable of being certainly identified. They admit of a further classification in regard to their respective contents. (1.) Four are entirely extracted from other authors. (2.) Six are partly original and partly selected. (3.) Nine are mostly selected from previous publications of their own, with a few from other authors intermixed. While(4.) Thirty- eight are strictly and exclusively original. This fourth and largest class constitutes the basis of the present edition, along with three volumes of the second class which it has been deemed advisable to reprint entire, because in the majority of instances the selected poems have been altered and adapted by the Editors for a purpose of their own, and according to their own taste. The third class, like the first, it is obviously unnecessary to include. With these reprints, there will be published in successive volumes a large number of poems left by Mr. Charles Wesley in MSS., and carefully revised for publication, but which, for some reason or reasons unknown, were not published by him; together with such single poems, whether in print already or in manuscript, as may not have been before collected the whole forming as complete a collection as circumstances will permit of the poetry of these wonderful and blessed men. Such a collection has been long desired by the lovers of sacred song in various parts of the world, as well as by "the people called Methodists," whose obligations to these two poets it is hard, if not impossible, adequately to express in words. Why the accomplishment of this wide-spread and earnest desire has been so long postponed, need not now be particularly considered, even were it practicable to state the various causes of the delay. Rather let the reader be invited to join the Editor in the earnest hope and prayer that the purpose so long cherished, and now at length in course of accomplishment, may be sanctioned by the Divine blessing, and that these "winged words" may carry with them everywhere those hallowing influences which it was the highest ambition of the writers to multiply and diffuse. It is only needful at present to add, that the volume now in the reader's hands contains a complete reprint of the two first of the poetical publications which bear the names of John and Charles Wesley. They were issued in rapid succession, doubtless to meet the wants of the infant Societies; and contain a larger number of selected and adapted poems than any of the subsequent volumes, except those entitled "A Collection of Psalms and Hymns," and "A Collection of Moral and Sacred Poems," neither of which will be reprinted entire. From those "Collections" the originals, as far as they can be ascertained, will be extracted for this edition; but to have pursued that course with the volumes of 1739 and 1740 would have been to destroy their identity, and to deprive the reader of many valuable and edifying pieces not easily accessible otherwise. Those "altered from Herbert," for instance, are only to be found in full in the volume of 1739; and, apart from their devotional character, supply interesting instances of the literary skill and judgment of the Wesleys. Even the fondest admirers of that holy ecclesiastic can scarcely be displeased at his appearance in a somewhat modernized attire, especially when they remember how much the Wesleys contributed to keep up his name and fame in an age when he was by no means so popular as now. The fine poems of Gambold were preserved and kept in circulation by the Wesleys; if, indeed, they do not entirely owe their publicity to the care and taste of the two brothers; not having been published by himself at all, nor by his friends until half a century after this volume appeared. The hymns of the venerable father of the Wesleys were likewise first collected by his sons in their first joint publication, and are thus made generally known.The two volumes now reprinted were each originally divided into two parts; and the division has been preserved here, though the reason of it cannot be ascertained. The volume of 1739 reached a third edition before that year expired; a fourth was published in 1743, and a fifth in 1756. To the fourth and fifth editions the volume of 1740 was added, its two parts being then numbered the third and fourth respectively, and the preface appearing in the third part. This composite volume was subsequently known and catalogued as Vol. 1 of "Hymns and Sacred Poems by John and Charles Wesley." A copy of it corrected for a new edition is in the possession of the Editor, and such corrections as have not been followed in the text of this volume are preserved in the notes. The only other alterations to be mentioned are, that the Index and Table of Contents are here adapted to the continuous paging; and that certain poems, afterwards published by their authors in other volumes, are transferred to the places to which they more properly belong; the transfer being mentioned as on pp. 269 and 289. To have omitted them from those later publications would have been unjust to the authors, and to have inserted them twice for the sake of an exact and literal reprint would have been unjust to the purchaser.

texts.4.1: Some verses, it may be observed, in the following Collection, were wrote upon the scheme of the Mystic divines. And these, 'tis owned, we had once in great veneration, as the best explainers of the Gospel of Christ. But we are now convinced that we therein greatly erred, not knowing the Scriptures, neither the power of God. And because this is an error which many serious minds are sooner or later exposed to, and which indeed most easily besets those who seek the Lord Jesus in sincerity; we believe ourselves indispensably obliged in the presence of God, and angels, and men, to declare wherein we apprehend those writers not to teach the truth as it is in Jesus.
texts.4.2: And first, we apprehend them to lay another foundation. They are careful indeed to pull down our own works, and to prove, that by the Deeds of the law shall no flesh be justified. But why is this? Only, to establish our own righteousness in the place of our own works. They speak largely and well against expecting to be accepted of God for our virtuous actions; and then teach, that we are to be accepted for our virtuous habits or tempers. Still the ground of our acceptance is placed in ourselves. The difference is only this Common writers suppose we are to be justified for the sake of our outward righteousness. These suppose we are to be justified for the sake of our inward righteousness: whereas, in truth, we are no more justified for the sake of one than of the other. For neither our own inward nor outward righteousness is the ground of our justification. Holiness of heart, as well as holiness of life, is not the cause, but the effect of it. The sole cause of our acceptance with God (or, that for the sake of which, on the account of which, we are accepted) is the righteousness and the death of Christ, who fulfilled God's law, and died in our stead. And even the condition of it is not (as they suppose) our holiness either of heart or life but our faith alone; faith contradistinguished from holiness as well as from good works. Other foundation therefore can no man lay, without being an adversary to Christ and His Gospel, than faith alone, faith, though necessarily producing both, yet not including either good works or holiness.
texts.4.3: But supposing them to have laid the foundation right, the manner of building thereon which they advise is quite opposite to that prescribed by Christ. He commands to build up one another. They advise, "To the desert, to the desert, and God will build you up." Numberless are the commendations that occur in all their writings, not of retirement intermixed with conversation, but of an entire seclusion from men, (perhaps for months or years,) in order to purify the soul. Whereas, according to the judgment of our Lord, and the writings of His apostles, it is only when we are knit together, that we have nourishment from Him, and increase with the increase of God. Neither is there any time when the weakest member can say to the strongest, or the strongest to the weakest, "I have no need of thee." Accordingly our blessed Lord, when His disciples were in their weakest state, sent them forth, not alone, but two by two. When they were strengthened a little, not by solitude, but by abiding with Him and one another, He commanded them to wait, not separate, but being assembled together, for the promise of the Father. And they were all with one accord in one place, when they received the gift of the Holy Ghost. Express mention is made in the same chapter, that when there were added unto them three thousand souls, all that believed were together, and continued steadfastly not only in the apostles' doctrine, but also in fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in praying with one accord. Agreeable to which is the account the great apostle gives of the manner which he had been taught of God, for the perfecting of the saints, for the edifying of the body of Christ, even to the end of the world. And, according to St. Paul, all who will ever come, in the unity of the faith, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ, must together grow up into Him from whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted (or strengthened) by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love. (Ephesians 4:15, 16.)
texts.4.4: So widely distant is the manner of building up souls in Christ taught by St. Paul, from that taught by the Mystics Nor do they differ as to the foundation, or the manner of building thereon, more than they do with regard to the superstructure. For the religion these authors would edify us in is solitary religion. If thou wilt be perfect, say they, "trouble not thyself about outward works. It is better to work virtues in the will. He hath attained the true resignation, who hath estranged himself from all outward works, that God may work inwardly in him, without any turning to outward things. These are the true worshippers, who worship God in spirit and in truth." For contemplation is with them the fulfilling of the law, even a contemplation that "consists in a cessation of all works."
texts.4.5: Directly opposite to this is the Gospel of Christ. Solitary religion is not to be found there. "Holy solitaries" is a phrase no more consistent with the Gospel than holy adulterers. The Gospel of Christ knows of no religion, but social; no holiness, but social holiness. Faith working by love is the length and breadth and depth and height of Christian perfection. This commandment have we from Christ, that he who loves God, love his brother also; and that we manifest our love by doing good unto all men, especially to them that are of the household of faith. And, in truth, whosoever loveth his brethren not in word only, but as Christ loved him, cannot but be zealous of good works. He feels in his soul a burning, restless desire of spending and being spent for them. My Father, will he say, worketh hitherto, and I work and, at all possible opportunities, he is, like his Master, going about doing good.
texts.4.6: This then is the way: walk ye in it, whosoever ye are that have believed in His name. Ye know, other foundation can no man lay, than that which is laid, even Jesus Christ. Ye feel that by grace ye are saved through faith; saved from sin, by Christ formed in your hearts, and from fear, by His Spirit bearing witness with your spirit, that ye are the sons of God. Ye are taught of God, not to forsake the assembling of yourselves together, as the manner of some is; but to instruct, admonish, exhort, reprove, comfort, confirm, and every way build up one another. Ye have an unction from the Holy One, that teacheth you to renounce any other or higher perfection, than faith working by love, faith zealous of good works, faith as it hath opportunity doing good unto all men. As ye have therefore received Jesus Christ the Lord, so walk ye in Him rooted and built up in Him, and stablished in the faith, and abounding therein more and more. Only, beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ. For ye are complete in Him. He is Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, the first and the last. Only continue in Him, grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the Gospel; and when Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear, with Him in glory.

W., makes it highly probable that, though his name is not prefixed, Wesley knew them to be the productions of his early friend. Clement's Description of a perfect Christian will be found in the Fourth Book of his "Stromata," or Miscellanies.

texts.5.2021: This translation from Gerhard Tersteegen (1697-1769) was made by Wesley while he was at Savannah, in 1736, and printed in "Psalms and Hymns," 1738. The original, beginning "Verborgne Gottes Liebe du", may be found in the Herrnhuth Collection, 1737, p. 483. That translation agrees with this, except in v. 4, where we read:Ah tear it thence, that Thou aloneMay'st reign unrivall'd Monarch there:From earthly loves I must be freeEre I can find repose in Thee. But after the ever-memorable 24th of May, 1738, Wesley knew "the way of God more perfectly;" and wrote as in the text. In a final revision for the "Large Hymn-Book," 1780, he changed "Be" in v.2, l.4, into "Seem," and made the closing couplet of v.8 precatory, in accordance with the two preceding, by changing "is" in the last line into "be."

texts.5.2030: Ah! why mistrust His will to save?
texts.5.2031: What meant that faltering of my heart?
texts.5.2033: That fill'd my coward flesh with fear;
texts.5.2036: Of hope I felt no joyful ground,
texts.5.2038: Naked of Christ my soul I found,
texts.5.2039: And started from a God unknown,
texts.5.2040: Corrupt my will, nor half subdued,
texts.5.2041: Could I His purer presence bear?
texts.5.2043: Could I before His face appear?
texts.5.2044: Father of mercies, hear my call!
texts.5.2045: Ere yet returns the fatal hour,
texts.5.2046: Repair my loss, retrieve my fall,
texts.5.2047: And raise me by Thy quickening power.
texts.5.2049: Be Thou my life, my hope, my gain;
texts.5.2051: And Death shall shake his dart in vain.
texts.5.2052: When I Thy promised Christ have seen,
texts.5.2053: And clasp'd Him in my soul's embrace,
texts.5.2055: Then, let me, Lord, depart in peace!
texts.5.2057: And live I yet by power Divine?
texts.5.2058: And have I still my course to run?
texts.5.2059: Again brought back in its decline
texts.5.2060: The shadow of my parting sun?
texts.5.2061: Wondering I ask, Is this the breast
texts.5.2062: Struggling so late and torn with pain?
texts.5.2063: The eyes that upward look'd for rest,
texts.5.2064: And dropt their weary lids again?
texts.5.2066: O, may they never cease to awe!
texts.5.2067: Still be the King of Terrors near,
texts.5.2068: Whom late in all his pomp I saw.
texts.5.2069: Torture and sin prepared his way,
texts.5.2070: And pointed to a yawning tomb!
texts.5.2072: And check'd my forward hopes of home.
texts.5.2073: My feeble flesh refused to bear
texts.5.2075: When Mercy heard my speechless prayer,
texts.5.2076: And saw me faintly gasp for ease.
texts.5.2078: Where sunk in mortal pangs I lay:
texts.5.2079: Pale Death his ancient Conqueror knew,
texts.5.2080: And trembled, and ungrasp'd his prey!
texts.5.2081: The fever turn'd its backward course,
texts.5.2084: And anguish gnaw'd my side no more.
texts.5.2085: God of my life, what just return
texts.5.2086: Can sinful dust and ashes give?
texts.5.2087: I only live my sin to mourn,
texts.5.2088: To love my God I only live!
texts.5.2089: To Thee, benign and saving Power,
texts.5.2091: While mark'd with blessings, every hour
texts.5.2093: How shall I teach the world to love,
texts.5.2095: Give me the power of faith to prove,
texts.5.2096: And mercy shall be all my song.
texts.5.2097: Be all my added life employ'd
texts.5.2098: Thy image in my soul to see:
texts.5.2099: Fill with Thyself the mighty void;
texts.5.2100: Enlarge my heart to compass Thee!
texts.5.2101: O, give me, Saviour, give me more!
texts.5.2102: Thy mercies to my soul reveal:
texts.5.2103: Alas! I see their endless store,
texts.5.2104: Yet, O! I cannot, cannot feel!
texts.5.2105: The blessing of Thy love bestow:
texts.5.2106: For this my cries shall never fail;
texts.5.2107: Wrestling, I will not let Thee go,
texts.5.2108: I will not, till my suit prevail.
texts.5.2109: I'll weary Thee with my complaint;
texts.5.2110: Here at Thy feet for ever lie,
texts.5.2111: With longing sick, with groaning faint:
texts.5.2112: O, give me love, or else I die!
texts.5.2114: 'Tis death, 'tis worse than death to live;
texts.5.2115: 'Tis hell to want Thy blissful face,
texts.5.2116: And saints in Thee their heaven receive.
texts.5.2117: Come then, my Hope, my Life, my Lord,
texts.5.2118: And fix in me Thy lasting home!
texts.5.2119: Be mindful of Thy gracious word,
texts.5.2120: Thou with Thy promised Father, come!
texts.5.2121: Prepare, and then possess my heart;
texts.5.2122: O, take me, seize me from above:
texts.5.2123: Thee do I love, for God Thou art;
texts.5.2124: Thee do I feel, for God is love!
texts.5.2126: Father of Lights, from whom proceeds
texts.5.2129: Feeds the young ravens when they cry;
texts.5.2130: To Thee I look: my heart prepare;
texts.5.2131: Suggest, and hearken to my prayer.
texts.5.2132: Since by Thy light myself I see
texts.5.2133: Naked, and poor, and void of Thee,
texts.5.2134: Thine eyes must all my thoughts survey,
texts.5.2135: Preventing what my lips would say:
texts.5.2136: Thou seest my wants; for help they call;
texts.5.2137: And ere I speak, Thou know'st them all.
texts.5.2138: Thou know'st the baseness of my mind,
texts.5.2140: Thou know'st how unsubdued my will,
texts.5.2141: Averse to good, and prone to ill;
texts.5.2142: Thou know'st how wide my passions rove,
texts.5.2143: Nor check'd by fear, nor charm'd by love.
texts.5.2144: Fain would I know, as known by Thee,
texts.5.2145: And feel the indigence I see;
texts.5.2146: Fain would I all my vileness own,
texts.5.2147: And deep beneath the burden groan;
texts.5.2148: Abhor the pride that lurks within,
texts.5.2149: Detest and loathe myself and sin.
texts.5.2150: Ah, give me, Lord, myself to feel;
texts.5.2152: Ah, give me, Lord, (I still would say,)
texts.5.2153: A heart to mourn, a heart to pray:
texts.5.2154: My business this, my only care,
texts.5.2155: My life, my every breath be prayer.
texts.5.2156: Scarce I begin my sad complaint,
texts.5.2157: When all my warmest wishes faint;
texts.5.2158: Hardly I lift my weeping eye,
texts.5.2159: When all my kindling ardours die;
texts.5.2160: Nor hopes nor fears my bosom move,
texts.5.2161: For still I cannot, cannot love.
texts.5.2162: Father, I want a thankful heart;
texts.5.2163: I want to taste how good Thou art;
texts.5.2164: To plunge me in Thy mercy's sea,
texts.5.2165: And comprehend Thy love to me,--
texts.5.2166: The breadth, and length, and depth, and height
texts.5.2168: Father, I long my soul to raise,
texts.5.2169: And dwell for ever on Thy praise;
texts.5.2170: Thy praise with glorious joy to tell,
texts.5.2172: While the full power of FAITH I know,
texts.5.2175: Who hath believed the tidings? Who?
texts.5.2176: Or felt the joys our words impart?
texts.5.2178: And found the Saviour in his heart?
texts.5.2181: There shall the Immortal Seed be found,
texts.5.2182: The Root Divine shall flourish there.
texts.5.2183: See the Desire of Nations comes,
texts.5.2184: Nor outward pomp bespeaks Him near:
texts.5.2185: A veil of flesh the God assumes,
texts.5.2186: A servant's form He stoops to wear.
texts.5.2187: He lays His every glory by;
texts.5.2189: Of beauty void, in reason's eye,
texts.5.2190: The Source of Loveliness is seen.
texts.5.2192: A Man of griefs, inured to woe;
texts.5.2194: And grief is all His life below.
texts.5.2195: We saw, and from the irksome sight
texts.5.2197: Hell follow'd Him with fierce despite,
texts.5.2198: And earth the humble Object scorn'd.
texts.5.2199: Surely for us He humbled was,
texts.5.2200: And grieved with sorrows not His own:
texts.5.2201: Of all His woes were we the cause,
texts.5.2202: We fill'd His soul with pangs unknown.
texts.5.2203: Yet Him the Offender we esteem'd,
texts.5.2206: And punish'd by an angry God.
texts.5.2207: But, O! with our transgressions stain'd,
texts.5.2208: For our offence He wounded was;
texts.5.2209: Ours were the sins that bruised and pain'd
texts.5.2210: And scourged, and nail'd Him to the cross.
texts.5.2211: The chastisement that bought our peace,
texts.5.2212: To sinners due, on Him was laid:
texts.5.2213: Conscience, be still! Thy terrors cease!
texts.5.2214: The debt's discharged, the ransom's paid.
texts.5.2215: What though we all as wandering sheep
texts.5.2216: Have left our God, and loved to stray,
texts.5.2217: Refused His mild commands to keep,
texts.5.2218: And madly urged the downward way?
texts.5.2219: Father, on Him Thy bolt did fall,
texts.5.2220: The mortal law Thy Son fulfill'd,
texts.5.2221: Thou laid'st on Him the guilt of all,
texts.5.2222: And by His stripes we all are heal'd.
texts.5.2223: Accused, His mouth He open'd not;
texts.5.2224: He answer'd not, by wrongs oppress'd.
texts.5.2225: Pure though He was from sinful spot,
texts.5.2227: Meek as a lamb to slaughter led,
texts.5.2228: A sheep before His shearers dumb,
texts.5.2229: To suffer in the sinner's stead
texts.5.2231: Who could His heavenly birth declare,
texts.5.2232: When bound by man He silent stood;
texts.5.2233: When worms arraign'd Him at their bar,
texts.5.2234: And doom'd to death the Eternal God!
texts.5.2237: Guiltless He groan'd and died for man:
texts.5.2238: Sinners, rejoice, He died for you!
texts.5.2239: For your imputed guilt He bled,
texts.5.2240: Made sin a sinful world to save;
texts.5.2241: Meekly He sunk among the dead:
texts.5.2242: The rich supplied an honour'd grave!
texts.5.2243: For, O! devoid of sin, and free
texts.5.2245: No sinner in Himself was He,
texts.5.2247: Yet Him the Almighty Father's will
texts.5.2249: Doom'd Him the weight of sin to feel,
texts.5.2250: And, sternly just, required His blood.
texts.5.2251: But, lo! the mortal debt is paid,
texts.5.2253: His soul, for sin an offering made,
texts.5.2254: Revives, and He shall die no more.
texts.5.2255: His numerous seed He now shall see,
texts.5.2256: Scatter'd through all the earth abroad,
texts.5.2258: Begot by Him, and born of God.
texts.5.2259: Head to His Church o'er all below,
texts.5.2260: Long shall He here His sons sustain;
texts.5.2261: Their bounding hearts His power shall know,
texts.5.2262: And bless the loved Messiah's reign.
texts.5.2263: 'Twixt God and them He still shall stand,
texts.5.2264: The children whom His Sire hath given;
texts.5.2265: Their cause shall prosper in His hand,
texts.5.2266: While RIGHTEOUSNESS looks down from heaven:
texts.5.2267: While pleased He counts the ransom'd race,
texts.5.2268: And calls and draws them from above;
texts.5.2269: The travail of His soul surveys,
texts.5.2270: And rests in His redeeming love.
texts.5.2271: 'Tis done! My justice asks no more,
texts.5.2273: Their sins He in His body bore,
texts.5.2274: Their Surety all the debt has paid.
texts.5.2275: My Righteous Servant and My Son
texts.5.2277: And all who stoop to abjure their own,
texts.5.2279: Them shall He claim His just desert,
texts.5.2281: And many a contrite humble heart
texts.5.2282: Will I for His possession give.
texts.5.2283: Satan He thence shall chase away,
texts.5.2284: Assert His right, His foes o'ercome;
texts.5.2285: Stronger than hell, retrieve the prey,
texts.5.2286: And bear the spoil triumphant home.
texts.5.2287: For charged with all their guilt He stood,
texts.5.2289: For them He pour'd out all His blood,
texts.5.2290: Their Substitute, He died for them.
texts.5.2291: He died, and rose His death to plead,
texts.5.2293: And still I hear Him intercede,
texts.5.2294: And still He makes their claim to heaven.
texts.5.2296: "Looking unto Jesus, the Author and Finisher of our faith."
texts.5.2297: Weary of struggling with my pain,
texts.5.2298: Hopeless to burst my nature's chain,
texts.5.2299: Hardly I give the contest o'er,
texts.5.2300: I seek to free myself no more.
texts.5.2301: From my own works at last I cease,
texts.5.2302: God that creates must seal my peace;
texts.5.2303: Fruitless my toil and vain my care,
texts.5.2304: And all my fitness is despair.
texts.5.2305: Lord, I despair myself to heal:
texts.5.2306: I see my sin, but cannot feel;
texts.5.2307: I cannot, till Thy Spirit blow,
texts.5.2308: And bid the obedient waters flow.
texts.5.2309: 'Tis Thine a heart of flesh to give;
texts.5.2310: Thy gifts I only can receive:
texts.5.2311: Here then to Thee I all resign;
texts.5.2312: To draw, redeem, and seal is Thine.
texts.5.2313: With simple faith, to Thee I call,
texts.5.2314: My Light, my Life, my Lord, my All:
texts.5.2315: I wait the moving of the pool;
texts.5.2316: I wait the word that speaks me whole.
texts.5.2317: Speak, gracious Lord, my sickness cure,
texts.5.2320: And pour Thyself into my heart.
texts.5.2322: "The Scripture hath concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe."
texts.5.2323: Jesu, the Sinner's Friend, to Thee,
texts.5.2324: Lost and undone, for aid I flee,
texts.5.2325: Weary of earth, myself, and sin;
texts.5.2326: Open Thine arms, and take me in.
texts.5.2327: Pity and heal my sin-sick soul;
texts.5.2328: 'Tis Thou alone canst make me whole:
texts.5.2329: Fall'n, till in me Thine image shine,
texts.5.2330: And cursed I am, till Thou art mine.
texts.5.2331: Hear, Jesu, hear my helpless cry;
texts.5.2332: O, save a wretch condemn'd to die!
texts.5.2333: The sentence in myself I feel,
texts.5.2334: And all my nature teems with hell.
texts.5.2336: No more my tortured heart divide!
texts.5.2337: When shall this agony be o'er,
texts.5.2338: And the old Adam rage no more!
texts.5.2340: Awake, and bruise the serpent's head!
texts.5.2341: Tread down Thy foes, with power control
texts.5.2342: The beast and devil in my soul.
texts.5.2344: Dispose my heart by entering there!
texts.5.2345: 'Tis this alone can make me clean,
texts.5.2346: 'Tis this alone can cast out sin.
texts.5.2347: Long have I vainly hoped and strove
texts.5.2348: To force my hardness into love,
texts.5.2349: To give Thee all Thy laws require;
texts.5.2350: And labour'd in the purging fire.
texts.5.2352: Call'd the deep Mystic to my aid:
texts.5.2353: His boasted skill the brute refined,
texts.5.2354: But left the subtler fiend behind.
texts.5.2355: Frail, dark, impure, I still remain,
texts.5.2356: Nor hope to break my nature's chain:
texts.5.2357: The fond self-emptying scheme is past,
texts.5.2358: And, lo! constrain'd, I yield at last.
texts.5.2359: At last I own it cannot be
texts.5.2360: That I should fit myself for Thee:
texts.5.2361: Here then to Thee I all resign;
texts.5.2362: Thine is the work, and only Thine.
texts.5.2363: No more to lift my eyes I dare,
texts.5.2365: I have my punishment in view;
texts.5.2366: I feel a thousand hells my due.
texts.5.2367: What shall I say Thy grace to move?
texts.5.2368: Lord, I am sin,--but Thou art Love:
texts.5.2369: I give up every plea beside,
texts.5.2370: "Lord, I am damn'd,--but Thou hast died!"
texts.5.2371: While groaning at Thy feet I fall,
texts.5.2372: Spurn me away, refuse my call,
texts.5.2373: If love permit, contract Thy brow,
texts.5.2374: And, if Thou canst, destroy me now!
texts.5.2377: My soul before Thee prostrate lies,
texts.5.2378: To Thee, her Source, my spirit flies;
texts.5.2379: My wants I mourn, my chains I see:
texts.5.2380: O, let Thy presence set me free!
texts.5.2381: Lost and undone, for aid I cry;
texts.5.2382: In Thy death, Saviour, let me die!
texts.5.2383: Grieved with Thy grief, pain'd with Thy pain,
texts.5.2384: Ne'er may I feel self-love again.
texts.5.2385: Jesu, vouchsafe my heart and will
texts.5.2386: With Thy meek lowliness to fill;
texts.5.2387: No more her power let Nature boast,
texts.5.2388: But in Thy will may mine be lost.
texts.5.2389: In life's short day let me yet more
texts.5.2391: My mind must deeper sink in Thee,
texts.5.2392: My foot stand firm, from wandering free.
texts.5.2393: Ye sons of men, here nought avails
texts.5.2394: Your strength; here all your wisdom fails
texts.5.2395: Who bids a sinful heart be clean?
texts.5.2396: Thou only, Lord, supreme of men.
texts.5.2397: And well I know Thy tender love;
texts.5.2399: And well I know Thou stand'st by me,
texts.5.2400: Pleased from myself to set me free.
texts.5.2401: Still will I watch, and labour still
texts.5.2402: To banish every thought of ill;
texts.5.2403: Till Thou in Thy good time appear,
texts.5.2404: And sav'st me from the fowler's snare.
texts.5.2406: God will destroy the power of hell:
texts.5.2407: God from the land of wars and pain
texts.5.2408: Leads me where peace and safety reign.
texts.5.2409: One only care my soul shall know,--
texts.5.2410: Father, all Thy commands to do:
texts.5.2411: Ah! deep engrave it on my breast,
texts.5.2412: That I in Thee even now am blest.
texts.5.2413: When my warm'd thoughts I fix on Thee,
texts.5.2414: And plunge me in Thy mercy's sea,
texts.5.2415: Then even on me Thy face shall shine,
texts.5.2416: And quicken this dead heart of mine.
texts.5.2417: So even in storms my zeal shall grow;
texts.5.2418: So shall I Thy hid sweetness know;
texts.5.2419: And feel (what endless age shall prove)
texts.5.2420: That Thou, my Lord, my God, art Love!
texts.5.2421: "Hier legt mein Sinn sich vor dir nieder" by Dr. C. F. Richter, of Halle. (1676-1711.) Herrnhuth Collection, p. 724. Or Knapp's Evangelischer Liederschatz, p.716. See an interesting anecdote relating to the use of this hymn in Lockwood's "Memorials of Peter Bohler," pp.77-79.
texts.5.2424: Awake, sad heart, whom sorrows drown,
texts.5.2425: Lift up thine eyes, and cease to mourn,
texts.5.2427: Thy Saviour and thy joys return.
texts.5.2429: No more lament, and pine, and cry:
texts.5.2430: His death thou ever dost partake,
texts.5.2432: Arise; if thou dost not withstand,
texts.5.2434: O, break not from the gracious Hand,
texts.5.2435: Which, as it rises, raises thee.
texts.5.2436: Cheer'd by thy Saviour's sorrows rise;
texts.5.2437: He grieved, that thou may'st cease to grieve:
texts.5.2438: Dry with His burial-clothes thine eyes;
texts.5.2439: He died Himself, that thou may'st live!
texts.6.1: "Try me, O God, and seek the ground of my heart."
texts.6.3: My Friend before the throne of Love!
texts.6.4: If now for me prevails Thy prayer,
texts.6.5: If now I find Thee pleading there;
texts.6.6: If Thou the secret wish convey,
texts.6.7: And sweetly prompt my heart to pray;
texts.6.8: Hear, and my weak petitions join,
texts.6.10: Fain would I know my utmost ill,
texts.6.11: And groan my nature's weight to feel;
texts.6.12: To feel the clouds that round me roll,
texts.6.13: The night that hangs upon my soul,
texts.6.14: The darkness of my carnal mind,
texts.6.15: My will perverse, my passions blind,
texts.6.16: Scatter'd o'er all the earth abroad,
texts.6.19: My earnest suit present and gain,
texts.6.23: A sharper sense of hell within,
texts.6.24: A stronger struggling to get free,
texts.6.26: For Thee my spirit often pants,
texts.6.28: Drooping it soon neglects to aspire,
texts.6.30: No more Thy glory's skirts are seen,
texts.6.31: The world, the creature steals between;
texts.6.32: Heavenward no more my wishes move,
texts.6.33: And I forget that Thou art Love.
texts.6.34: O sovereign Love, to Thee I cry;
texts.6.35: Give me Thyself, or else I die.
texts.6.36: Save me from death, from hell set free;
texts.6.37: Death, hell, are but the want of Thee.
texts.6.39: Saved, when possest of Thee, I am;
texts.6.40: My life, my only heaven, Thou art:
texts.6.41: And, lo! I feel Thee in my heart!
texts.6.42: The Prayer-Book version is quoted here, as often elsewhere by the Wesleys. In the first edition the title prefixed to this piece was, "Blessed are they that mourn" (Matt. 5:4.). In the second and all subsequent editions it stands as above.
texts.6.43: In editions 2, 3, for "And, lo! I feel" we read, "When shall I feel?" and in editions 4 and 5, "O might I feel Thee in my heart."
texts.6.47: Though duteous to Thy high command,
texts.6.48: Not seraphs view with open face,
texts.6.49: But veil'd before Thy presence stand:
texts.6.50: How shall weak eyes of flesh, weigh'd down
texts.6.51: With sin, and dim with error's night,
texts.6.52: Dare to behold Thy awful throne,
texts.6.54: Restore my sight! let Thy free grace
texts.6.55: An entrance to the holiest give!
texts.6.56: Open my eyes of faith! Thy face
texts.6.57: So shall I see; yet seeing live.
texts.6.59: Reach forth: see, my whole heart I bow:
texts.6.60: Say to my soul, "Thou art my love,
texts.6.62: O Jesu, full of grace! the sighs
texts.6.63: Of a sick heart with pity view!
texts.6.64: Hark how my silence speaks; and cries,
texts.6.66: I know Thou canst not but be good!
texts.6.67: How shouldst Thou, Lord, Thy grace restrain?
texts.6.68: Thou, Lord, whose blood so largely flow'd
texts.6.69: To save me from all guilt and pain.
texts.6.70: Into Thy gracious hands I fall,
texts.6.71: And with the arms of faith embrace:
texts.6.72: King of Glory, hear my call!
texts.6.73: O, raise me, heal me by Thy grace!
texts.6.74: Now righteous through Thy wounds I am;
texts.6.76: I taste salvation in Thy Name,
texts.6.77: Alive in Thee my living Head!
texts.6.78: Still let Thy wisdom be my guide,
texts.6.79: Nor take Thy light from me away;
texts.6.80: Still with me let Thy grace abide,
texts.6.81: That I from Thee may never stray.
texts.6.82: Let Thy word richly in me dwell;
texts.6.83: Thy peace and love my portion be;
texts.6.84: My joy to endure and do Thy will,
texts.6.85: Till perfect I am found in Thee.
texts.6.86: Arm me with Thy whole armour, Lord,
texts.6.87: Support my weakness with Thy might;
texts.6.88: Gird on my thigh Thy conquering sword,
texts.6.89: And shield me in the threatening fight.
texts.6.90: From faith to faith, from grace to grace,
texts.6.91: So in Thy strength shall I go on,
texts.6.92: Till heaven and earth flee from Thy face,

texts.6.95: Wesley inserted this poem in "Moral and Sacred Poems," vol. 3, p.3, assigning it to his father as its author. He also reprinted it in the first volume of the Arminian Magazine. When the Monthly Reviewers disparaged Methodist hymns, he transcribed fifty lines of it, and sent them with a remonstrance against the criticism. (Works, 3rd edition, vol. 13, pp.345-349.) In some editions the verses are headed "From the Greek;" but Dr. Clarke has shown that this is an error. The copy printed in his "Wesley Family" contains eighty-four additional lines; but Wesley never published more than are given here.

texts.7.563: This, and the "Farewell to the World," p.17, were probably furnished to the compilers by Mr. Byrom of Manchester, (see "Byrom and the Wesleys," by the Rev. Dr. Hoole, pp.17, 27,) and translated by him from the French of Madame de Bourignon. The copy of "A Hymn to Jesus," which is found in his Miscellaneous Poems, (Manchester, 1773,) vol. 2, p.211, differs from that given above only in the title, and in such verbal alterations as the superior taste and judgment of the Wesleys would dictate. The 9th and 10th verses in both Byrom's and Wesley's copies are tinged with that mysticism to which the preface refers; and Wesley has improved on himself as well as on Byrom in the last edition of v.9, (that in the Large Hymn-Book, 1780,) where, instead of "Nor heaven nor earth," we read "Nothing on earth."

texts.9.319: In the first and third editions this hymn is entitled "Justified but not Sanctified." In the second edition it finds no place. In the fourth and fifth the title stands as above; and the change is wisely made, inasmuch as the distinction so clearly maintained in Wesley's later years between Sanctification and Entire Sanctification is overlooked in the original title, or dropped for the sake of antithesis. In the copy corrected for a sixth edition verse 9 is erased. Doubtless the editor felt that the tone of the last couplet was somewhat more familiar than he could approve, though the pathos and earnestness of the hymn have made it a general favourite from the beginning.

texts.9.488: Paul Gerhardt (1606-1676) is said by one of his German biographers to have had John Arndt's "Prayer and Paradise Garden" continually before him at the close of his life, and to have written "several hymns on its contents." To Arndt, therefore, as its ultimate source, we must trace the invaluable hymn before us; which, as written by Gerhardt, is found in No. 23 in the Herrnhuth Collection, and on p. 304 of Knapp's E. L.

texts.9.972: O Lord, O God of Love,
texts.9.974: King of all, with pitying eye
texts.9.975: Mark the toil, the pains we feel:
texts.9.976: 'Midst the snares of death we lie,
texts.9.980: Help us to obtain the prize,
texts.9.981: Help us well to close our race;
texts.9.982: That with Thee above the skies
texts.9.984: This noble composition was inserted by Wesley in his first book, 1738. It stands No. 68 in the Herrnhuth Collection, "Dich, Jesu, loben wir," and is given by Dr. Knapp as from the Pennsylvanian Collection of 1844, without any author's name. E. L., p.236.
texts.9.988: Haste; to Him who sends the light,
texts.9.990: Souls, put on your glorious dress,
texts.9.992: Clothed with Christ, aspire to shine.
texts.9.995: He in God, and God in Him!
texts.9.996: Strive we Him in us to see,
texts.9.998: Burst we then the bands of death,
texts.9.1000: Long we to be loosed from earth,
texts.9.1002: Spent at length is nature's night;
texts.9.1003: Christ attends to give us Light,
texts.9.1005: God we now may see, and live.
texts.9.1007: Form'd within us day by day
texts.9.1008: Still the Inner Man we view,
texts.9.1010: Turn, O turn us, Lord, again,
texts.9.1014: Thy great will in us be done:
texts.9.1016: Ours no longer let us be;
texts.9.1017: Hide us from ourselves in Thee!
texts.9.1018: Thou the Life, the Truth, the Way,
texts.9.1019: Suffer us no more to stray;
texts.9.1020: Give us, Lord, and ever give
texts.9.1021: Thee to know, in Thee to live!
texts.9.1022: A Morning Dedication of Ourselves to Christ
texts.9.1024: Jesu, Thy light again I view,
texts.9.1025: Again Thy mercy's beams I see,
texts.9.1026: And all within me wakes, anew
texts.9.1028: Again my thoughts to Thee aspire
texts.9.1029: In fervent flames of strong desire.
texts.9.1030: But, O! what offering shall I give
texts.9.1031: To Thee, the Lord of earth and skies?
texts.9.1032: My spirit, soul, and flesh receive
texts.9.1034: Small as it is, 'tis all my store
texts.9.1035: More shouldst Thou have, if I had more.
texts.9.1036: Now then, my God, Thou hast my soul;
texts.9.1037: No longer mine, but Thine I am:
texts.9.1038: Guard Thou Thy own; possess it whole,
texts.9.1039: Cheer it by hope, with love inflame.
texts.9.1040: Thou hast my spirit; there display
texts.9.1041: Thy glory to the perfect day.
texts.9.1042: Thou hast my flesh; Thy hallow'd shrine,
texts.9.1044: Here let Thy light for ever shine,
texts.9.1045: This house still let Thy presence fill:
texts.9.1046: O Source of Life, live, dwell, and move
texts.9.1047: In me, till all my life be love.
texts.9.1048: O, never in these veils of shame,
texts.9.1049: Sad fruits of sin, my glorying be!
texts.9.1050: Clothe with salvation through Thy name
texts.9.1051: My soul, and may I put on Thee!
texts.9.1052: Be living faith my costly dress,
texts.9.1053: And my best robe Thy righteousness!
texts.9.1054: Send down Thy likeness from above,
texts.9.1055: And let this my adorning be:
texts.9.1056: Clothe me with wisdom, patience, love,
texts.9.1058: Than gold and pearls more precious far,
texts.9.1059: And brighter than the morning star.
texts.9.1060: Lord, arm me with Thy Spirit's might,
texts.9.1061: Since I am call'd by Thy great name:
texts.9.1062: In Thee my wandering thoughts unite,
texts.9.1063: Of all my works be Thou the aim.
texts.9.1064: Thy love attend me all my days,
texts.9.1065: And my sole business be Thy praise!
texts.9.1066: From Dr. Joachim Lange, (1670-1744,) "O Jesu susses licht." Herrnhuth Collection, No.308. Knapp, E.L., p.1018.
texts.9.1069: O Jesu, source of calm repose,
texts.9.1070: Thy like nor man nor angel knows,
texts.9.1072: Even those whom death's sad fetters bound,
texts.9.1074: Find light and life, if Thou appear.
texts.9.1076: Ere rolling planets knew to shine,
texts.9.1077: Ere time its ceaseless course began;
texts.9.1078: Thou, when the appointed hour was come,
texts.9.1079: Didst not abhor the Virgin's womb,
texts.9.1080: But, God with God, wert Man with man.
texts.9.1081: The world, sin, death oppose in vain;
texts.9.1082: Thou, by Thy dying, death hast slain,
texts.9.1083: My great Deliverer, and my God!
texts.9.1084: In vain does the old dragon rage,
texts.9.1085: In vain all hell its powers engage;
texts.9.1086: None can withstand Thy conquering blood.
texts.9.1087: Lord over all, sent to fulfil
texts.9.1089: To Thy dread sceptre will I bow:
texts.9.1090: With duteous reverence at Thy feet,
texts.9.1091: Like humble Mary, lo, I sit:
texts.9.1092: Speak, Lord! Thy servant heareth now.
texts.9.1093: Renew Thy image, Lord, in me,
texts.9.1094: Lowly and gentle may I be;
texts.9.1095: No charms but these to Thee are dear:
texts.9.1096: No anger mayst Thou ever find,
texts.9.1097: No pride in my unruffled mind,
texts.9.1098: But faith and heaven-born peace be there.
texts.9.1100: That, life and all things cast behind,
texts.9.1101: Springs forth obedient to Thy call,
texts.9.1102: A heart that no desire can move,
texts.9.1103: But still to adore, believe, and love,
texts.9.1104: Give me, my Lord, my Life, my All.
texts.9.1105: From J. A. Freylinghausen, (1670-1739,) "Wer ist wol wie Du." Herrn. Coll., No.30. Knapp, E. L., p.137.
texts.9.1108: O God of God, in whom combine
texts.9.1109: The heights and depths of love Divine,
texts.9.1110: With thankful hearts to Thee we sing!
texts.9.1111: To Thee our longing souls aspire
texts.9.1112: In fervent flames of strong desire:
texts.9.1113: Come, and Thy sacred unction bring.
texts.9.1114: All things in earth and air and sea
texts.9.1115: Exist and live and move in Thee;
texts.9.1116: All Nature trembles at Thy voice:
texts.9.1117: With awe even we Thy children prove
texts.9.1118: Thy power. O, let us taste Thy love!
texts.9.1120: O powerful Love, to Thee we bow,
texts.9.1121: Object of all our wishes Thou,
texts.9.1122: (Our hearts are naked to Thine eye,)
texts.9.1123: To Thee, who from the eternal throne
texts.9.1124: Cam'st emptied of Thy Godhead down,
texts.9.1125: For us to groan, to bleed, to die.
texts.9.1126: Grace we implore; when billows roll,
texts.9.1127: Grace is the anchor of the soul;
texts.9.1128: Grace every sickness knows to heal:
texts.9.1129: Grace can subdue each fond desire,
texts.9.1130: And patience in all pain inspire,
texts.9.1132: O Love, our stubborn wills subdue,
texts.9.1134: Dispel our darkness by Thy light:
texts.9.1135: Into all truth our spirit guide,
texts.9.1136: But from our eyes for ever hide
texts.9.1137: All things displeasing in Thy sight.
texts.9.1138: Be heaven even now our soul's abode,
texts.9.1139: Hid be our life with Christ in God,
texts.9.1140: Our spirit, Lord, be one with Thine:
texts.9.1141: Let all our works in Thee be wrought,
texts.9.1142: And fill'd with Thee be all our thought,
texts.9.1143: Till in us Thy full likeness shine.
texts.9.1144: The original is said to be a hymn by Count Zinzendorf, ("Gott aus dem quilt altes Leben"} which has not yet been identified.
texts.9.1147: Come, and in me delight to rest!
texts.9.1148: Drawn by the lure of strong desire,
texts.9.1149: O, come, and consecrate my breast:
texts.9.1150: The temple of my soul prepare,
texts.9.1151: And fix Thy sacred presence there!
texts.9.1152: If now Thy influence I feel,
texts.9.1153: If now in Thee begin to live,
texts.9.1154: Still to my heart Thyself reveal;
texts.9.1155: Give me Thyself, for ever give.
texts.9.1156: A point my good, a drop my store:
texts.9.1157: Eager I ask, and pant for more.
texts.9.1158: Eager for Thee I ask and pant,
texts.9.1160: Carries me out with sweet constraint,
texts.9.1161: Till all my hallow'd soul be Thine:
texts.9.1162: Plunged in the Godhead's deepest sea,
texts.9.1164: My peace, my life, my comfort now,
texts.9.1165: My treasure, and my all Thou art!
texts.9.1166: True witness of my sonship Thou,
texts.9.1168: Seal of my sins in Christ forgiven,
texts.9.1169: Earnest of love, and pledge of heaven.
texts.9.1170: Come then, my God, mark out Thy heir,
texts.9.1171: Of heaven a larger earnest give,
texts.9.1172: With clearer light Thy witness bear;
texts.9.1174: Let all my powers Thy entrance feel,
texts.9.1175: And deeper stamp Thyself the seal.
texts.9.1177: Come, and in me delight to rest!

texts.9.1184: When Christ had left His flock below,
texts.9.1185: The loss His faithful flock deplored:

texts.9.1187: And languish for their absent Lord.

texts.9.1189: Gifts to receive, and claim His crown,
texts.9.1190: Beheld them sorrowing from His sky,
texts.9.1191: And pour'd the mighty blessing down.
texts.9.1192: He, for the presence of His flesh,
texts.9.1194: And living streams their souls refresh,
texts.9.1195: And joy Divine o'erflows their hearts.
texts.9.1196: While all, in sweet devotion join'd,
texts.9.1197: Humbly to wait for God retire,
texts.9.1198: The promised grace in rushing wind
texts.9.1199: Descends, and cloven tongues of fire.

texts.9.1201: The feeble dome beneath Him shook.
texts.9.1202: Trembled the crowd to feel Him come,
texts.9.1203: Soon as the sons of thunder spoke.

texts.9.1205: To us and ours the promise made,
texts.9.1206: To us be graciously the same,
texts.9.1207: And crown with living fire our head.
texts.9.1208: Our claim admit, and from above
texts.9.1211: And zeal and unity and power.
texts.9.1214: Such as may every conscience reach,
texts.9.1217: Searching the inmost of the mind,
texts.9.1218: To purge all fierce and foul desire,
texts.9.1219: And kindle life more pure and kind:
texts.9.1220: The Spirit of faith, in this Thy day,
texts.9.1221: To break the power of cancell'd sin,
texts.9.1222: Tread down its strength, o'erturn its sway,
texts.9.1223: And still the conquest more than win.
texts.9.1224: The Spirit breathe of inward life,
texts.9.1225: Which in our hearts Thy laws may write:

texts.9.1228: On all the earth Thy Spirit shower,
texts.9.1230: Thy kingdom come, and hell's o'erpower,
texts.9.1231: And to Thy sceptre all subdue.
texts.9.1232: Like mighty wind, or torrent fierce,
texts.9.1234: And every law of sin reverse,
texts.9.1235: That faith and love may make all one.
texts.9.1236: Yea, let Thy Spirit in every place
texts.9.1238: While lovely tempers, fruits of grace,
texts.9.1239: The kingdom of Thy Christ prepare.
texts.9.1240: Grant this, O holy God, and true!
texts.9.1241: The ancient seers Thou didst inspire:
texts.9.1242: To us perform the promise due;
texts.9.1243: Descend, and crown us now with fire.

texts.9.1247: Lo, God is here! Let us adore,
texts.9.1248: And own how dreadful is this place!
texts.9.1249: Let all within us feel His power,
texts.9.1250: And silent bow before His face.
texts.9.1251: Who know His power, His grace who prove,
texts.9.1252: Serve Him with awe, with reverence love.
texts.9.1253: Lo, God is here! Him day and night
texts.9.1254: The united choirs of angels sing:
texts.9.1255: To Him enthroned above all height
texts.9.1256: Heaven's hosts their noblest praises bring:
texts.9.1257: Disdain not, Lord, our meaner song,
texts.9.1258: Who praise Thee with a stammering tongue.
texts.9.1259: Gladly the toys of earth we leave,
texts.9.1260: Wealth, pleasure, fame, for Thee alone:
texts.9.1261: To Thee our will, soul, flesh we give;
texts.9.1262: O take, O seal them for Thy own!
texts.9.1263: Thou art the God; Thou art the Lord:
texts.9.1264: Be Thou by all Thy works adored!
texts.9.1265: Being of beings, may our praise
texts.9.1266: Thy courts with grateful fragrance fill;
texts.9.1267: Still may we stand before Thy face,
texts.9.1268: Still hear and do Thy sovereign will.
texts.9.1269: To Thee may all our thoughts arise,
texts.9.1271: In Thee we move. All things of Thee
texts.9.1272: Are full, Thou Source and Life of all!
texts.9.1274: Fall prostrate, lost in wonder, fall,
texts.9.1275: Ye sons of men; for God is man!
texts.9.1276: All may we lose, so Thee we gain!
texts.9.1277: As flowers their opening leaves display,
texts.9.1278: And glad drink in the solar fire,
texts.9.1279: So may we catch Thy every ray,
texts.9.1280: So may Thy influence us inspire:
texts.9.1281: Thou Beam of the Eternal Beam,
texts.9.1282: Thou purging Fire, Thou quickening Flame!

texts.9.1284: Prayer to Christ Before the Sacrament

texts.9.1290: To Thee our humblest thanks we pay,
texts.9.1291: To Thee our souls we bow;
texts.9.1292: Of hell erewhile the helpless prey,
texts.9.1294: As incense to Thy throne above,
texts.9.1296: O, wing with flames of holy love
texts.9.1298: Stir up Thy strength, O Lord of Might,

texts.9.1315: Sons of God, and heirs of heaven!

texts.9.1322: Heal'd and quicken'd by His blood,

texts.9.1329: Purged its guilt, dissolved its power;

texts.9.1343: Ours the heaven of perfect love!

texts.9.1347: In many a soul the Saviour stirr'd,

texts.9.1350: With them in mighty prayer combined,

texts.9.1354: And deeds of wonder, guards His flock;

texts.9.1416: How wide Thy healing streams are spread!
texts.9.1417: With whom dost Thou delight to dwell?

texts.9.1419: O God what tongue aright can tell

texts.9.1421: The dictates of Thy sovereign will
texts.9.1422: With joy our grateful hearts receive:
texts.9.1423: All Thy delight in us fulfil;
texts.9.1424: Lo! all we are to Thee we give.
texts.9.1425: To Thy sure love, Thy tender care,

texts.9.1428: And seal the abode for ever Thine.

texts.9.1431: Yea, even our crimes, though numberless,
texts.9.1432: Less numerous than Thy mercies are.

texts.9.1434: Still may we pant Thy Son to know!
texts.9.1435: Thy Spirit still breathe into our breast,
texts.9.1436: Fountain of peace and joy below!

texts.9.1438: Since from the world Thou mad'st us free:
texts.9.1439: Still may we praise Thee more and more,
texts.9.1440: Our hearts more firmly knit to Thee!
texts.9.1441: Still, Lord, Thy saving health display,

texts.9.1450: Thy sovereign light within my heart,

texts.11.1: By grace, saith St. Paul, ye are saved through faith. And it is indeed a great salvation which they have received who truly believe on the name of the Son of God. It is such as eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man to conceive, until God hath revealed it by His Spirit, which alone showeth these deep things of God.
texts.11.2: Of this salvation the prophets inquired diligently, searching what manner of time the Spirit which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow; even that glorious liberty from the bondage of corruption which should then be given to the children of God. Much more doth it behove us, diligently to inquire after this prize of our high calling, and earnestly to hope for the grace which is brought unto us by the revelation of Jesus Christ.
texts.11.3: Some faint description of this gracious gift of God is attempted in a few of the following verses. But the greater part of them relate to the way, rather than the end; either showing (so far as has fallen under our observation) the successive conquests of grace, and the gradual process of the work of God in the soul; or pointing out the chief hindrances in the way, at which many have stumbled and fallen.
texts.11.4: This great gift of God, the salvation of our souls, which is begun on earth, but perfected in heaven, is no other than the Image of God fresh stamped upon our hearts. It is a renewal in the spirit of our minds after the likeness of Him that created us. It is a salvation from sin and doubt and fear: From Fear; for, being justified freely, they who believe have peace with God through Jesus Christ our Lord, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. From Doubt; for the Spirit of God beareth witness with their spirit, that they are the children of God And from Sin; for being now made free from sin, they are become the servants of righteousness.
texts.11.5: God hath now laid the axe to the root of the tree, purifying their hearts by faith, and cleansing all the thoughts of their hearts by the inspiration of His Holy Spirit. Having this hope, that they shall soon see God as He is, they purify themselves even as He is pure; and are holy as He which hath called them is holy in all manner of conversation. Not that they have already attained all they shall attain, either are already (in this sense) perfect. But they daily go on from strength to strength beholding now as in a glass the glory of the Lord, they are changed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.
texts.11.6: And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty; such liberty from the law of sin and death as the children of this world will not believe, though a man declare it unto them. The Son hath made them free, and they are free indeed insomuch that St. John lays it down, as a first principle among true believers, We know that whosoever is born of God sinneth not: but he that is begotten of God keepeth himself, and that wicked one toucheth him not. And again, Whosoever abideth in Him (in CHRIST) sinneth not. And yet again, Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin. For his seed remaineth in him, and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.
texts.11.7: The Son hath made them free, who are thus born of God, from that great root of sin and bitterness, Pride. They feel, that all their sufficiency is of God; that it is He alone who is in all their thoughts, and worketh in them both to will and to do of His good pleasure. They feel, that it is not they who speak, but the Spirit of their Father which speaketh in them; and that whatsoever is done by their hands, the Father which is with them, He doeth the works. So that God is to them all in all, and they are as nothing in His sight. They are freed from self-will; as desiring nothing, no, not for one moment, (for perfect love casteth out all desire,) but the holy and perfect will of God: not supplies in want; not ease in pain; not life or death, or any creature; but continually crying in their inmost soul, "Father, Thy will be done." They are freed from evil thoughts, so that they cannot enter into them; no, not for one instant. Aforetime, when an evil thought came in, they looked up, and it vanished away. But now it does not come in; there being no room for this in a soul which is full of God. They are freed from wanderings in prayer. Whensoever they pour out their hearts in a more immediate manner before God, they have no thought of anything past or absent, or to come, but of God alone; to whom their whole souls flow in one men stream, and in whom they are swallowed up. In times past, they had wandering thoughts darted in; which yet fled away like smoke. But now that smoke does not rise at all, but they continually see Him which is invisible. They are freed from all darkness, having no fear, no doubt, either as to their state in general; or as to any particular action: for their eye being single, their whole body is full of light. Whatsoever is needful, they are taught of God. They have an unction from the Holy One, which abideth in them, and teacheth them every hour, what they shall do, and what they shall speak. Nor have they therefore any need to reason concerning it; for they see the way straight before them. The Lamb is their light, and they simply follow Him, whithersoever He goeth. Hence also they are, in one sense, freed from temptations; for though numberless temptations fly about them, yet they wound them not, they trouble them not, they have no place in them. At all times their soul is even and calm; their heart is steadfast and immovable; their peace, flowing as a river, passeth all understanding, and they rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. For they are sealed by the Spirit unto the day of redemption; having the witness in themselves, that there is laid up for them a crown of righteousness, which the Lord shall give them in that day; and being fully persuaded, through the Holy Ghost, that neither death nor life, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate them from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus, their Lord.
texts.11.8: Not that every one is a child of the devil (as some have rashly asserted, who know not what they speak, nor whereof they affirm) till he is, in this full sense, born of God. On the contrary, whosoever he be, who hath a sure trust and confidence in God, that through the merits of Christ his sins are forgiven, and he reconciled to the favour of God; he is a child of God, and, if he abide in Him, an heir of all the great and precious promises. Neither ought he in any wise to cast away his confidence, or to deny the faith he hath received, because it is weak, because hitherto it is only as a grain of mustard-seed; or because it is tried with fire, so that his soul is in heaviness through manifold temptations. For though the heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, yet is he lord of all. God doth not despise the day of small things; the day of fears, and doubts, and clouds: but if there be first a willing mind, pressing toward the mark of the prize of our high calling, it is accepted (for the present) according to what a man hath, and not according to what he hath not.
texts.11.9: Neither therefore dare we affirm (as some have done) that this full salvation is at once given to true believers. There is indeed an instantaneous (as well as a gradual) work of God in the souls of His children; and there wants not, we know, a cloud of witnesses, who have received in one moment, either a clear sense of the forgiveness of their sins, or the abiding witness of the Holy Spirit. But we do not know a single instance, in any place, of a person's receiving, in one and the same moment, remission of sins, the abiding witness of the Spirit, and a new, a clean heart.
texts.11.10: Indeed how God may work, we cannot tell; but the general manner wherein He does work is this. Those who once trusted in themselves that they were righteous, who were rich and had need of nothing, are, by the Spirit of God applying His word, convinced that they are poor and naked. All the things that they have done are brought to their remembrance, and set in array before them; so that they see the wrath of God hanging over their heads, and feel they deserve the damnation of hell. In their trouble they cry unto the Lord, and He shows He hath taken away their sins, and opens the kingdom of heaven in their hearts, even righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. Fear and sorrow and pain are fled away, and sin hath no more dominion over them. Knowing they are justified freely through faith in His blood, they have peace with God through Jesus Christ; they rejoice in hope of the glory of God, and the love of God is shed abroad in their hearts.
texts.11.11: In this peace they remain for days, or weeks, or months, and commonly suppose they shall not know war any more, till some of their old enemies, their bosom sins, or the sin which did most easily beset them, (perhaps anger or desire,) assault them again, and thrust sore at them, that they may fall. Then arises fear, that they shall not endure to the end; and often doubt, whether God has not forgotten them, or whether they did not deceive themselves, in thinking their sins were forgiven, and that they were children of God. Under these clouds, especially if they reason with the devil, or are received to doubtful disputations, they go mourning all the day long, even as a father mourneth for his only son whom he loveth. But it is seldom long before their Lord answers for Himself, sending them the Holy Ghost, to comfort them, to bear witness continually with their spirit, that they are the children of God. And then they are indeed meek, and gentle, and teachable, even as little children. Their stony heart was broken in pieces before they received remission of sins yet it continued hard; but now it is melted down, it is soft, tender, and susceptible of any impression. And now first do they see the ground of their heart; which God would not before disclose unto them, lest the flesh should fail before Him, and the spirit which He had made. Now they see all the hidden abominations there; the depths of pride, self-will, and hell. Yet having the witness in themselves, "Thou art an heir of God, a joint heir with Christ; thou shalt inherit the new heavens and the new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness;" their spirit rejoiceth in God their Saviour, even in the midst of this fiery trial, which continually heightens both the strong sense they then have of their inability to help themselves, and the inexpressible hunger they feel after a full renewal in His image, in righteousness, and all true holiness. Then God is mindful of the desire of them that fear Him: He remembers His holy covenant, and He giveth them a single eye and a clean heart. He stamps upon them His own image and superscription: He createth them anew in Christ Jesus: He cometh unto them with His Son and His blessed Spirit, and, fixing His abode in their souls, bringeth them into the rest which remaineth for the people of God.

texts.12.713: The animating strains of this hymn and the two next are by no means in accordance with Charles Wesley's spiritual condition and mood of mind in December, 1737, when Mr. Whitefield first left England for America. They were more probably composed in preparation for his second voyage, which began in August, 1739. Nor can we imagine anything more suitable for the occasion; while in the hymns "To be Sung at Sea," and "In a Storm," the Christian and the poet appear to equal advantage. It may be doubted if the full assurance of faith was ever more finely expressed, or at the same time more rationally vindicated, than in the second and third of the three hymns which follow one another here.

texts.31.103: By heart conceived it cannot be,
texts.31.104: The bliss Thou hast for him prepared
texts.31.105: Who waits in humble faith for Thee.
texts.31.106: Thou meetest him that dares rejoice
texts.31.107: In hope of Thy salvation near;
texts.31.108: Who wants, while he obeys Thy voice,
texts.31.109: The perfect love that casts out fear;
texts.31.111: Who Thee remembers in Thy ways,--
texts.31.113: The sacred channels of Thy grace.
texts.31.114: But, lo! Thy anger kindled is,
texts.31.115: And justly might for ever burn;
texts.31.116: We have forsook the path of peace:
texts.31.117: How shall our wandering souls return?
texts.31.118: In Thine appointed ways we wait,
texts.31.119: The ways Thy wisdom hath enjoin'd;
texts.31.120: Thy saving grace we here shall meet,
texts.31.121: If every one that seeks shall find.
texts.31.122: Nor can we thus Thy wrath appease;
texts.31.123: We and our works are all unclean,
texts.31.125: Our good is ill, our virtue sin.
texts.31.126: Like wither'd leaves we fade away;
texts.31.127: We all deserve Thy wrath to feel;
texts.31.128: Swift as the wind, our sins convey
texts.31.129: And sweep our guilty souls to hell.
texts.31.130: Not one will call upon Thy name,
texts.31.131: Stir himself up Thy grace to see,
texts.31.132: The LORD his righteousness to claim,
texts.31.133: And boldly to take hold on Thee.
texts.31.134: For, O! Thy face is turn'd aside,
texts.31.135: Since we refused to obey Thy will;
texts.31.136: Thou hast consumed us for our pride,
texts.31.137: Thy heavy hand consumes us still.
texts.31.138: But art Thou not our Father now?
texts.31.139: Our Father now Thou surely art:
texts.31.140: Humbly beneath Thy frown we bow,
texts.31.141: We seek Thee with a trembling heart.
texts.31.142: The Potter Thou, and we the clay;
texts.31.143: Behold us at Thy footstool laid;
texts.31.144: In anger cast us not away,
texts.31.145: The creatures whom Thy hands have made.
texts.31.146: O, let Thine anger rage no more,
texts.31.148: See, LORD, and all our sins pass o'er,
texts.31.152: A den of thieves Thy temple is,
texts.31.153: No longer now the house of prayer.
texts.31.154: Where humbly low our fathers bow'd,
texts.31.155: And Thee with joyful lips adored,
texts.31.157: And take the altar for its LORD.
texts.31.160: By these blasphemed, by those profaned,
texts.31.161: Our pleasant things are all laid waste.
texts.31.162: And wilt Thou not this havoc see,
texts.31.163: For which we ever, ever mourn?
texts.31.164: Still shall we cry in vain to Thee?
texts.31.166: Hold not Thy peace at Sion's woe;
texts.31.167: O, cast not out Thy people's prayer;
texts.31.169: And spare, the weeping remnant spare.
texts.31.172: That all mankind may sing Thy praise,
texts.31.173: Thou God of Truth, Thou God of Love.
texts.31.175: "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God."
texts.31.176: Lord, I believe a rest remains,
texts.31.178: A rest where pure enjoyment reigns,
texts.31.180: A rest where all our soul's desire
texts.31.182: Where doubt, and pain, and fear expire,
texts.31.184: A rest of lasting joy and peace,
texts.31.186: 'Tis then from our own works we cease,
texts.31.188: Our life is hid with Christ in God;
texts.31.190: We wrestle not with flesh and blood,
texts.31.191: We strive with sin no more.
texts.31.192: Our spirit is right, our heart is clean,
texts.31.194: We cannot now, we cannot sin,
texts.31.195: For we are born of God.
texts.31.198: On all the powers of hell we tread,
texts.31.200: Redeem'd, we walk on holy ground,
texts.31.201: On God we cast our care;
texts.31.202: No lion in that way is found,
texts.31.204: Safe in the way of life, above
texts.31.205: Death, earth, and hell we rise;
texts.31.206: We find, when perfected in love,
texts.31.210: It guards us, as a wall of fire,
texts.31.211: And as a sword of flame.
texts.31.212: O that I now the rest might know,
texts.31.214: Now, Saviour, now the power bestow,
texts.31.215: And let me cease from sin.
texts.31.216: Remove this hardness from my heart,
texts.31.218: To me the rest of faith impart,
texts.31.220: I groan from pride to be set free,
texts.31.222: Take me, O, take me into Thee,
texts.31.224: I would be Thine, Thou know'st I would,
texts.31.225: And have Thee all my own;
texts.31.228: Thy Name to me, Thy Nature grant;
texts.31.230: Nothing besides my God I want,
texts.31.232: Come, O my Saviour, come away,
texts.31.234: No longer from Thy creature stay,
texts.31.236: The bliss Thou hast for me prepared
texts.31.239: For whom I first was made.
texts.31.240: Come, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost,
texts.31.242: Let all I am in Thee be lost,
texts.31.243: Let all I am be God!
texts.31.244: Wesley found, under the pressure of controversy, (Works, vol. 10, p.397,) if not sooner, that these expressions were indefensible; and marked verses 4 and 5 to be omitted in future editions.
